conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m Claire, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s a quick, 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, so we can give you the best support possible.

Everything we discuss stays between us unless safety becomes a concern, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll take it one question at a time; each focuses on the past seven days.

Ready to begin?

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

(small half-shrug, eyes on the baby blanket in my lap)

Um…sometimes? Like, if my partner makes a joke while we’re folding laundry I might smile, but it feels kind of forced. Nothing feels really “funny” these days—more like I’m too tired to laugh, even when I know something’s supposed to be amusing.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Hmm… not really. I might give a little chuckle if my partner pulls a silly face, but it’s like the laugh doesn’t reach my stomach the way it used to. Things that should feel funny just feel flat—like I’m going through the motions.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much. I mean, I still get the baby dressed every morning and I tell myself, “Today we’ll go for a walk and maybe get a coffee,” but by the time I’ve packed the diaper bag I’m already worn out. The idea of doing anything I used to enjoy—like meeting a friend or even just watching a show—feels more like a chore than something to look forward to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a couple of times. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking, “I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not reading his cues right.” I know rationally it’s probably just a phase, but the thought still pops up that if I were better at this, he’d sleep easier and I wouldn’t feel so drained.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most days, yeah. It’s like there’s a low hum of worry running in the background even when everything looks fine on the outside. I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly my heart’s racing, imagining he’s too quiet or that I missed a dirty diaper and he’ll get a rash. I check his breathing a couple of times a night—no real reason, just can’t shake the fear that something might go wrong.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full-on panicky… more like a sudden wave of “what if something bad happens and I’m not ready?” It’ll hit when I’m just folding onesies—my chest gets tight, I feel kind of shaky, and I have to sit down and breathe on purpose. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me jittery for a while.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… I feel like I’m treading water most of the day. There’s always a bottle to wash, laundry piling up, the baby needs changing just when I finally sit to eat. I start one chore, notice two others, and end up forgetting what I began. By evening I’m exhausted but still feel I didn’t accomplish anything, and I go to bed with that restless “I’m already behind for tomorrow” feeling.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s not so much being unhappy—more like my head won’t stop buzzing. I lie down and replay every little thing I did that day: Did I burp him long enough? Was that red spot on his cheek there before? I’ll check the monitor, adjust the volume, then stare at the ceiling for ages. Takes me at least an hour to drift off most nights, and when he wakes up I struggle to fall back asleep even after he’s settled.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… it kind of drifts in and out. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel this heaviness, like I’m about to cry, but then it backs off. I’m not weepy all day, just these moments when everything feels gray and I miss the version of me who used to feel lighter.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really. I get that thick-throat feeling a couple of times a day, but actual tears—maybe twice this week. Once when I couldn’t get the stroller unfolded in the parking lot and cars were lining up behind me. I just stood there biting my lip, eyes watering, but I swallowed hard and pushed the tears down. Mostly the sadness stays inside, heavy but quiet.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I feel tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like “me” again so I can be there for my baby.

You have bravely shared how the joy of new motherhood feels clouded by a persistent heaviness and worry. Over the past week laughter has felt forced, activities you once enjoyed now seem burdensome, and a steady stream of self-doubt and background anxiety leaves you exhausted yet unable to rest. Even simple tasks feel like "treading water," and moments of sadness drift in uninvited, yet you remain devoted to your baby and hopeful of returning to yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 20, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports markedly reduced laughter and describes humour feeling flat, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-complete loss of anticipatory pleasure; even planning simple activities feels burdensome, matching "Hardly at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a couple of times" linked to baby's nap trouble, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, daily background worry and intrusive anxious thoughts/racing heart despite no objective concern, matching 'very often'.</sym>, <sym>The patient describes sudden, unexpected episodes of anxiety with physical symptoms (tight chest, shakiness) that require active coping, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive overwhelm and inability to manage daily tasks, matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent nighttime rumination and delayed sleep onset, matching 'Yes, sometimes' even though she attributes it to anxiety rather than unhappiness.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, noticeable waves of sadness and tearfulness that intrude during routine tasks, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score of 20 meets the EPDS threshold (≥14) indicating probable <med>postpartum depression</med> with co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. Core symptoms align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: diminished interest/pleasure (<quote>feels more like a chore</quote>), depressed mood (<quote>everything feels gray</quote>), self-blame, fatigue, concentration difficulty, and sleep disruption. Anxiety items (Q4,5) scored maximum points, highlighting prominent <sym>generalized worry</sym> and episodic <sym>panic-type sensations</sym>. Functional impact is moderate to severe (<quote>I go to bed with that restless 'I'm already behind for tomorrow' feeling</quote>). Denial of self-harm keeps safety risk low today. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> to discuss results and consider therapy and/or medication options
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or <med>psychologist</med> trained in CBT or interpersonal therapy for postpartum depression
3. Share these EPDS results and your descriptions of <sym>low mood</sym> and <sym>anxiety</sym> so clinicians can formulate a treatment plan
4. Enlist practical help: accept offers of housework, meals, or night-time bottle feeds to improve rest; aim for at least one 4-hour block of uninterrupted sleep
5. Practice daily 5-minute breathing or mindfulness exercises when the baby naps to reduce <sym>background anxiety</sym> and support emotional regulation
6. Schedule gentle outdoor activity (short walk with stroller) most days; light movement and sunshine can modestly lift mood
7. Plan a follow-up EPDS in 2-3 weeks with your provider to monitor progress after interventions are started
8. Keep emergency numbers handy (national crisis line, your clinic) should <sym>low mood</sym> worsen or self-harm thoughts ever develop
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 20: Screening note – Postpartum visit

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, sense of emotional “flatness”  
- Marked loss of pleasure/interest (anhedonia) re previously enjoyed activities  
- Excessive self-blame and guilt regarding infant care  
- Nearly daily, non-specific anxiety and situational panic symptoms  
- Sleep-onset difficulty driven by rumination  
- Frequent feeling of being overwhelmed, “treading water,” difficulty completing tasks

Pattern  
Symptoms present most days, interfere with daily functioning and caregiving, no discrete triggers identified.

Risk factors/significance  
- Meets screening criteria for probable postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety  
- Denies self-harm or suicidal ideation (safety concern absent at present)  
- Functional impairment moderate (fatigue, task incompletion, social withdrawal)

Plan  
Provide results, offer education, recommend formal clinical evaluation for mood/anxiety disorder and appropriate intervention options.
